sections.title: 🔍 Why architecture is a discipline, not a component
paras: The same chip can top a benchmark, sip power in a phone, or excel at graphics. How fast a transistor switches is fixed by the fabrication process, but how those transistors are organised is a design decision. Computer architecture is the study of that organisation and of the interfaces it exposes.

There is no single best answer, because the constraints conflict. Going faster means doing more in parallel, which costs complexity and power. Saving power means lower frequency and voltage, which costs performance. Staying compatible with old software means carrying instructions nobody would design today. Architecture is the art of picking a point in that space.

sections.title: ⚙️ Architecture vs. organisation: what vs. how
paras: Textbooks separate the two terms sharply and the separation matters for everything that follows.

Architecture (also called the instruction set architecture, ISA) is what a programmer can see: which instructions exist, how many registers there are, how large the address space is, how data types are represented. It is the contract between software and hardware, and changing it breaks binaries.

Organisation (microarchitecture) is how a particular chip honours that contract: the pipeline depth, the cache sizes, how many instructions issue per cycle, how branch prediction works. Two processors with the same ISA can differ by a factor of three in speed.
bullets: The ISA changes rarely, because every change fragments the software ecosystem.
The microarchitecture changes every generation, and it is where most performance gains come from.
A programmer optimising in C is typically targeting the microarchitecture while assuming the ISA.
An operating system kernel touches the ISA directly: page tables, interrupt vectors, privileged instructions.
Compilers sit exactly on the boundary: they emit ISA instructions and are tuned against real microarchitectures.

sections.title: 🧮 From one line of Python to transistors
paras: Take the line a = b + c. How many layers of abstraction does it cross before it becomes a voltage?

Layer 1: the Python compiler turns the source into bytecode, an instruction such as BINARY_ADD. Layer 2: the CPython interpreter loop executes that bytecode and calls into C. Layer 3: the C function operates on PyObject pointers and reads a type slot. Layer 4: the compiler has turned that C into x86 or ARM machine code. Layer 5: the processor decoder splits each machine instruction into micro-operations, and each micro-operation is a set of control signals. Layer 6: the control signals drive logic gates in the ALU. Layer 7: each gate is a handful of transistors switching.
bullets: Each layer depends only on the abstraction the layer below offers, never on how it is implemented.
That is why Python can feel slow while the CPU is fast: they are being measured at different layers.
One Python addition can become dozens of machine instructions (type checks, object allocation, reference counting).
Profiling a Python loop therefore measures the interpreter, not the adder.
The ISA boundary sits between layer 4 and layer 5, which is why it is the layer that both compilers and hardware designers must agree on.

sections.title: 🔍 Why put programs in the same memory as data
paras: Early computers were wired for one job. To run a different calculation you physically rewired the machine or reloaded a plugboard, which took hours. The stored-program idea removes that: keep the instructions in memory as numbers, and changing the program becomes changing memory contents.

The consequence is enormous and easy to underrate. A computer becomes general purpose, because the sequence of operations is data that the machine can read, copy, and even generate. Compilers, interpreters, and just-in-time translation all depend on programs being ordinary bytes.

sections.title: ⚙️ Four subsystems, one shared bus
paras: The model has four parts and they are worth naming precisely, because every later chapter refers back to them.
bullets: Memory holds both instructions and data, in one address space, addressed by number.
The control unit fetches the next instruction, decodes it, and emits the signals that drive everything else.
The ALU performs the arithmetic and logic the instruction asks for.
Input and output move bytes between memory and the outside world.
Because instructions and data share one path to memory, every instruction fetch competes with every data read: this is the von Neumann bottleneck.
The bottleneck is not a defect to be fixed but a constraint to be worked around, and caches, pipelines, and prefetchers are all workarounds.

sections.title: 🧮 Counting the trips across that single bus
paras: Suppose three instructions: load a value, add a constant, store the result. In the simplest implementation, each instruction takes two memory trips: one to fetch the instruction itself, and one for its data operand. That is six trips for three instructions.

Now add a multiply that needs two operands from memory. Each operand is a separate trip, so that instruction costs three trips instead of two. In a sequence of 100 instructions where one third touch two operands, the total is about 233 trips rather than 200: roughly 17 percent overhead purely from operand traffic.

If each trip takes 80 nanoseconds at 12.5 MHz, 233 trips is 18.6 microseconds. If you want that program to run four times faster, you cannot get there by making the adder faster, because the adder is idle most of the time. You have to reduce the number of trips, which is exactly what a cache does: keep the hot instructions and operands close, and most accesses stop crossing the shared bus at all.

sections.title: 🔍 Why a loop instead of a burst
paras: A CPU has no notion of a program. It has a counter and a rule: read what the counter points at, do it, move the counter on. Everything a computer appears to do is that rule repeated.

The loop shape explains a lot of behaviour that otherwise looks strange. An infinite loop is not a special state: it is the counter being set back to an earlier address forever. A crash is often the counter reaching an address that holds bytes which are not a valid instruction.

sections.title: ⚙️ The five stages and the registers that carry state
paras: The canonical cycle has more stages than the four-word version suggests, and each stage has a register to hold its intermediate result.

Fetch reads the instruction at the program counter into the instruction register. Decode determines which operation it is and which operands it names. Execute performs the operation, usually in the ALU. Memory access reads or writes an operand if the instruction needs it. Write-back puts the result into a register.
bullets: The program counter holds the address of the next instruction, not the current one.
The instruction register holds the instruction currently being decoded.
Decode is not optional: the bit pattern must be interpreted before anything can be executed.
The program counter advances during fetch, which is why a jump has to overwrite it rather than add to it.
A single instruction can take several clock cycles, so one cycle per instruction is the wrong mental model.
Modern CPUs overlap the stages of different instructions, so the register values belong to different instructions at the same moment.

sections.title: 🧮 A cycle budget by hand
paras: Assume a classic multi-cycle machine where fetch takes 1 cycle, decode 1, execute 1, memory access 1, and write-back 1. A register-to-register add needs no memory stage, so it costs 4 cycles. A load costs 5, because it uses the memory stage.
A loop that runs 10 times, with 3 register adds and 1 load in the body, costs 10 x (3 x 4 + 1 x 5) = 170 cycles, plus a few for the compare and the jump. At 1 GHz that is 0.17 microseconds.

Now the same code on a 5-stage pipeline running at 1 GHz: the first instruction takes 5 cycles to finish, but after that one instruction retires per cycle while nothing stalls. About 40 instructions then take 5 + 39 = 44 cycles, roughly four times fewer than 170. The pipeline did not make any individual instruction faster. It overlapped them, which is why throughput and latency have to be discussed separately.

sections.title: 🔍 Why base 2, and why hex in every debugger
paras: A wire carries a voltage and a transistor is a switch. Two stable states are cheap to build and cheap to distinguish; ten stable voltage levels are neither. Binary is therefore not a stylistic choice, it is what the physics makes reliable.

Hexadecimal exists only for human eyes. A byte written in binary is eight characters that all look alike, and reading a 64-bit address in binary is hopeless. Because 16 is a power of two, four bits map onto exactly one hex digit with no arithmetic, so hex is binary with the spacing fixed.

sections.title: ⚙️ Place value, nibbles, and the two power-of-two scales
paras: Binary works like decimal with a different base: each position is worth a power of two, and the rightmost is 2 to the power 0. Converting to decimal means adding the weights where a 1 appears. Converting to hex means grouping the bits in fours from the right and replacing each group with one character.
The memory-size prefixes need care because two conventions exist and the difference is large at scale.
bullets: Group from the right: 1101 0110 is D6, not 6D.
One hex digit is four bits; one byte is two hex digits, so a 32-bit address is exactly eight hex digits.
A KiB is 1024 bytes and a KB is 1000 bytes; a 1 TiB disk is about 1.1 TB, which is where the missing capacity in a new drive comes from.
Memorising 2 to the power 10 as 1024, 2 to the power 20 as about one million, and 2 to the power 30 as about one billion makes most sizing questions mental arithmetic.
Bit positions are numbered from 0 at the least significant end, so bit 7 of a byte is its leftmost bit.

sections.title: 🧮 Conversions you can do in your head
paras: Binary 1011: 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11. Hex 2F: 2 x 16 + 15 = 47. Going the other way, 47 in binary: the largest power of two not exceeding 47 is 32, leaving 15, then 8 leaving 7, then 4 leaving 3, then 2 leaving 1, then 1, giving 101111.
For hex, split 47 into nibbles: 47 = 2 x 16 + 15, so the digits are 2 and F. Check the grouping: 0010 1111 is indeed 47.

Now a size calculation. A chip has 20 address lines. That is 2 to the power 20 = 1,048,576 addresses, and if each address is one byte, 1 MiB. With 32 address lines it is 4 GiB, which is why 32-bit machines could not address more than 4 GB per process without extra machinery.
A last one that trips people up: 0x1000 is not 1000 decimal. It is 4096, the boundary at which many tools report memory. A buffer overrun of 16 bytes past 0x1000 lands in the next page.

sections.title: 🔍 Why one zero forces an asymmetric range
paras: With n bits there are 2 to the n distinct patterns, and they must cover positive numbers, negative numbers, and zero. The naive approach of using one bit as a sign gives two zeros: plus zero and minus zero. Two patterns that compare equal but are not identical is a bug factory.

Two's complement spends one pattern on zero and leaves the remaining 2 to the n minus 1 patterns split unevenly, so the negative side gets one extra value. That asymmetry is not an oversight; it is the price of a single zero, and it is why the most negative number has no positive counterpart.

sections.title: ⚙️ Flip, add one, and let addition do the work
paras: To negate a value in two's complement, invert every bit and add one. The elegance is that the adder does not need to know whether its inputs are signed: the same circuit that adds two unsigned numbers adds two signed numbers correctly, which is why one ALU serves both.

Sign extension is the other half of the trick: widening a signed value copies its top bit into the new positions, while widening an unsigned value fills with zeros. Get that wrong and a small negative number becomes a huge positive one.
bullets: 4 bits give the range minus 8 to plus 7; 8 bits give minus 128 to plus 127; 32 bits give roughly minus 2.1 billion to plus 2.1 billion.
The top bit is part of the value, not a separate magnitude flag, so reading it as a sign flag and the rest as magnitude gives wrong answers.
Overflow is not an error, it wraps silently: adding 1 to the largest positive value produces the most negative value.
Detection rule: overflow happened when the carry into the sign bit differs from the carry out of it.
Two's complement subtraction is addition of the negation, so there is no separate subtract circuit.

sections.title: 🧮 Working the arithmetic by hand
paras: Plus 5 in 4 bits is 0101. Invert: 1010. Add 1: 1011, which is minus 5. Check by adding back: 0101 + 1011 = 1 0000, and the carry out of 4 bits is discarded, leaving 0000. Zero, as required.

So what is 1011 worth? Its top bit is 1, so it is negative. Take the magnitude: invert to 0100, add 1, get 0101 = 5, so the value is minus 5. The shortcut is to read 1011 as minus 8 plus 0 plus 2 plus 1 = minus 5.

Now overflow. With 4 bits, 0111 is 7. Add 0001: 1000, which reads as minus 8. The arithmetic wrapped; a program counting up from 7 and testing for a positive value would loop forever or read out of bounds. With 8 bits the same error appears at 127 + 1 = minus 128.

Mixed widths cost real money: 8 bits can hold 255, 16 bits hold 65,535, 32 bits hold about 4.29 billion. An image with 70,000 pixels per row overflows a 16-bit coordinate type, which is why large image libraries use 32-bit indices.

sections.title: 🔍 Why fixed-point runs out of range
paras: Integer representations put the binary point at the right edge, so the smallest step is 1 and the largest value is bounded by the bit width. Move the point left and you gain fractions but lose range. Neither arrangement can cover both an electron mass and a national debt in the same 32 bits.

Floating point solves it by storing the position of the point as part of the number. The cost is that the spacing between representable values is not constant: near 1 the steps are tiny, near a trillion they are large.

sections.title: ⚙️ Three fields and a hidden bit
paras: IEEE 754 single precision packs 32 bits into three fields: one sign bit, eight exponent bits, and twenty-three fraction bits. Double precision is one, eleven, and fifty-two.

The stored exponent carries a bias of 127 (single) or 1023 (double), so that exponents can be compared as if they were unsigned. The leading 1 of the normalised significand is not stored, which buys one extra bit of precision for free.
bullets: Single precision gives about 7 significant decimal digits; double gives about 16.
The exponent range for double is roughly 10 to the minus 308 up to 10 to the 308.
Special patterns encode zero, infinity, and not-a-number, which is why dividing by zero produces an infinity rather than a trap.
Rounding is round-to-nearest-even by default, so repeated operations drift slowly rather than systematically.
Comparing floats with equality is unsound; compare the absolute difference against a tolerance.

sections.title: 🧮 Encoding a value and watching the error grow
paras: Encode 6.75. In binary it is 110.11, normalised as 1.1011 times 2 to the power 2. The exponent field is 2 + 127 = 129, which is 10000001. The fraction field holds the bits after the leading 1: 1011 followed by zeros. The stored word is 0 10000001 1011000 and the rest zeros.
Decode 0.5: it is 1.0 times 2 to the power minus 1, exponent field 126, fraction all zeros. Very clean, because 0.5 is exactly representable.

Now 0.1. It is 1.6 times 2 to the power minus 4, and 0.6 in binary repeats forever, so the stored value is the nearest 24-bit approximation. The error is about 1.5 times 10 to the minus 9 in single precision.

That error compounds. Add 0.1 ten times in single precision and the result is not 1.0 but something like 1.0000001. Accumulate a million such additions in a loop and the drift reaches the hundredths, which is why financial code uses integers of cents or a decimal type rather than floats.
A second classic: 0.1 + 0.2 equals 0.30000000000000004 in double precision. The sum is correct to 16 digits but not exact, and an equality test against 0.3 fails.

sections.title: 🔍 Why gates are the whole alphabet
paras: A transistor is an electrically controlled switch. Put a few together and you can make a circuit whose output depends on its inputs according to a boolean rule. That is a logic gate, and it is the only primitive hardware gives you: everything above it is arrangement.

The surprising part is how few rules you need. AND, OR, and NOT are enough to express any boolean function, and NAND alone is also enough. That is why a fabrication plant can build a general-purpose processor from one repeated structure.

sections.title: ⚙️ Truth tables, universality, and what a gate costs
paras: A truth table lists the output for every input combination, so a two-input gate has four rows. A circuit with n inputs has 2 to the n rows, which is why truth tables are a design tool for small blocks and useless for whole processors.
Functional completeness means a single gate type can build every other. NAND is complete because NOT, AND, and OR can each be made from it, and those three can make anything.
bullets: AND outputs 1 only when all inputs are 1; OR outputs 1 when any input is 1; XOR outputs 1 when the inputs differ.
NAND is AND followed by NOT: output 0 only when all inputs are 1.
NOT from NAND: tie both inputs together.
AND from NAND: NAND followed by NOT, which is two NAND gates.
A CMOS NAND needs four transistors; a NOR needs four; an AND needs six because it is NAND plus an inverter.
Fan-out matters: one output driving many inputs slows down because of capacitance, which is why real chips buffer long signal paths.

sections.title: 🧮 Gate counting from a truth table
paras: Build XOR from NAND gates, since XOR is what an adder needs for each column. XOR of a and b is (a NAND (a NAND b)) NAND (b NAND (a NAND b)). That is four NAND gates, so four gates for one sum bit.

A one-bit half adder also needs a carry, which is simply a AND b, and that is one more NAND plus an inverter, so six gates in total. A full adder accepts a carry-in, so the sum is XOR of three inputs and the carry is the majority of three: nine NAND gates is the standard count.

Chain four full adders and you have a 4-bit ripple-carry adder: 36 gates. Each column must wait for the carry of the one to its right, so the delay is the carry delay times four. With a typical gate delay of 50 picoseconds that is 200 picoseconds, which sets a ceiling on the clock of about 5 GHz for that block alone.
That number is why real adders use carry-lookahead: computing the carries in parallel costs more gates but cuts the delay from linear to logarithmic, and 32-bit adders are built that way.

sections.title: 🔍 Why a circuit with no memory is useful
paras: If the output depended on history, the circuit would be impossible to test and impossible to reason about: the same inputs could give different results. Restricting to circuits whose output is a pure function of the current inputs gives blocks that can be specified by a truth table and verified exhaustively.

Almost everything in the datapath is combinational: adders, comparators, shifters, multiplexers, decoders. The parts that remember, registers and memory, are the exception, and separating the two is what makes processor design tractable.

sections.title: ⚙️ Adders, multiplexers, decoders, and the delay that limits the clock
paras: An adder takes two n-bit values and produces an n-bit sum plus a carry. The half adder handles two bits; the full adder adds a carry-in so that columns can be chained. A ripple-carry chain is simple and slow; a carry-lookahead version computes carries in parallel and is what real hardware uses.

A multiplexer selects one of several inputs under a control signal, and it is the hardware form of an if statement. A decoder does the inverse of selection: it takes an n-bit code and asserts exactly one of 2 to the n output lines, which is how memory addresses select a word.
bullets: A 2-to-1 multiplexer is three gates if built from AND, OR, and NOT.
An n-bit multiplexer with 2 to the k inputs needs k select lines.
A 3-to-8 decoder has 3 inputs and 8 outputs, exactly one of which is high at any time.
Ripple-carry delay grows linearly with width; carry-lookahead grows logarithmically.
Combinational circuits cannot hold a value, so any stored state must be a register outside the block.

sections.title: 🧮 Sizing a datapath by hand
paras: Suppose you want a 4-way selector between 8-bit values. You need two select lines, because 2 to the 2 is 4, and the multiplexer is 8 bits wide, so eight one-bit 4-to-1 multiplexers run in parallel.

Add two 8-bit numbers with a ripple-carry adder: eight full adders. The critical path runs through all eight carry stages. If a full adder's carry takes 60 picoseconds, the last sum bit is valid after about 480 picoseconds, so this block cannot run faster than roughly 2 GHz.

Now feed a 20-bit address into a decoder for a memory with one million words. The decoder has 2 to the 20 = 1,048,576 outputs, which is impractical as a flat circuit, so real memories decode in two stages: ten bits for the row and ten for the column, giving 1024 + 1024 lines instead of a million. That two-stage trick is exactly how DRAM chips are organised.

sections.title: 🔍 Why a bit needs feedback
paras: A combinational circuit forgets its input the moment the input goes away. To remember, an output must be routed back to an input, so the circuit holds itself in a stable state. That loop is the whole idea behind memory: a value that keeps reasserting itself until something forces a change.

The consequence is subtle and important. Feedback means a circuit can have more than one stable state for the same inputs, so it can no longer be described by a truth table alone; the behaviour depends on what it held before, which is exactly what memory is.

sections.title: ⚙️ Latches, flip-flops, registers, and cells
paras: A latch is level sensitive: while the enable signal is high, the output follows the input. A flip-flop is edge triggered: it captures the input only at a clock edge and holds it for the rest of the cycle. Modern designs use flip-flops because edge triggering makes timing analysis tractable: all state changes at one instant.

A register is a row of flip-flops sharing a clock and a load signal, so n bits update together. A memory array is a grid of single-bit cells with row and column decoders, which is what makes a large capacity affordable.
bullets: A D flip-flop has one data input, one clock, and one output: value in at the edge, held until the next edge.
Clock-to-output and setup time bound how fast a register can be clocked.
A 32-bit register is 32 flip-flops that must all meet the same setup time, which is why clock skew is a design problem.
SRAM cells (six transistors) hold a bit as long as power is on and are used for caches.
DRAM cells (one transistor plus one capacitor) are far denser but must be refreshed thousands of times per second.
A register file is a small array with multiple read ports, which is why reading two operands and writing one is possible in a single cycle.

sections.title: 🧮 Counting cells, lines, and cycles
paras: A 64-bit register is 64 flip-flops. A register file with 32 entries of 64 bits is 2048 flip-flops, plus the selection logic, which is why register files stay small: doubling the count doubles the area and slows the access path.

A memory with 2 to the 20 words needs 20 address lines. If it is organised as 1024 rows by 1024 columns, there are 1024 row select lines and 1024 column select lines, plus a 20-to-1048576 decoder replaced by two 10-to-1024 decoders.

Now timing. Suppose a flip-flop has a clock-to-output of 40 picoseconds, the logic between registers takes 200 picoseconds, and setup is 30 picoseconds. The minimum clock period is 270 picoseconds, so the maximum clock is about 3.7 GHz. Adding one more level of logic worth 100 picoseconds forces the clock down to about 2.7 GHz, which is the concrete trade a deeper pipeline makes.

sections.title: 🔍 Why one circuit serves every arithmetic instruction
paras: A processor could have a separate circuit for addition, one for subtraction, one for AND, and so on. In practice it has one ALU with many operations selected by a control code, because the alternative would multiply the area and the wiring for no gain: at any moment only one operation is running.

The ALU is where the abstraction of the ISA meets the gates. Every arithmetic and logic instruction in the instruction set is ultimately a value on the operation-select lines and a set of inputs from registers.

sections.title: ⚙️ The operation selector and the flags
paras: An ALU takes two operands, an operation code, and produces a result plus a set of status flags. The flags are the part that beginners miss: without them a conditional branch has nothing to test.

Zero means the result was all zeros. Negative is a copy of the result's top bit. Carry is the carry out of the top bit, meaningful for unsigned arithmetic. Overflow is set when the signed result does not fit, which is when the carry into the sign bit differs from the carry out.
bullets: Subtraction is addition with the second operand negated, so one adder serves both.
A typical ALU offers add, subtract, AND, OR, XOR, NOT, shift left, shift right, and compare, with compare being a subtraction whose result is discarded and whose flags are kept.
The result multiplexer selects among the operation outputs based on the operation code.
Flags are written to a status register, and the next conditional branch reads them.
The ALU's delay is the longest operation's delay, which is normally the carry chain of the adder.
Bitwise operations are per-bit and have no carries, so they are much faster than addition at the gate level.

sections.title: 🧮 Flags for two specific operations
paras: Add 200 and 100 as 8-bit unsigned. The sum is 300, which does not fit, so the stored result is 300 minus 256 = 44 and the carry flag is 1. The overflow flag stays 0, because overflow is a signed question and 200 is already outside the signed range. This is the trap: carry answers the unsigned question, overflow answers the signed one, and a program that checks the wrong flag misses the error entirely.

Do it properly with signed operands: 100 + 100 in 8 bits. The stored result is 200, which as a signed value is minus 56, because 200 is greater than 127. The carry out is 0 (no unsigned wrap) but the overflow flag is 1, since two positives produced a negative. A program that adds test scores and gets minus 56 has hit exactly this.

Now a subtraction that sets carry: 5 minus 10 in 8-bit unsigned. The second operand is negated to 246, the sum is 251 with a carry out of 1. In unsigned terms the carry out being 1 means a borrow occurred, which is why the borrow flag is often the complemented carry.

Delay check: if the carry chain of a 32-bit adder costs 25 picoseconds per bit, the adder needs 800 picoseconds, so an ALU built this way cannot feed a 2 GHz pipeline without being split across cycles.

sections.title: 🔍 Why control is separated from data
paras: The datapath knows how to add, select, and store, but it does not know when. Something has to decide that this cycle the ALU adds rather than compares, that the register file writes rather than reads, that memory is addressed rather than idle. That something is the control unit.

The split is not bureaucratic: it is the reason processor design is possible at all. The datapath can be designed for the worst case and then reused, while the control is a table of which signals to raise, and tables can be generated, verified, and extended.

sections.title: ⚙️ Hardwired versus microprogrammed
paras: There are two ways to build the decoder. A hardwired control unit is random logic that maps the opcode and the cycle counter directly onto control signals: fast, but rigid and painful to change. A microprogrammed control unit stores a small program per instruction, where each micro-instruction is a set of control signals; it is slower because it reads its own memory, but easier to extend, which is why complex instruction sets used it.
The clock is what turns the sequence into a schedule. Every stage completes within one period, and the control unit's job is to guarantee that no path is longer than the period.
bullets: Control signals include register enable, ALU operation code, memory read or write, and the selector for the write-back destination.
The cycle counter or state machine tells the control unit which step of the current instruction it is on.
A single-cycle design sets every signal combinationally from the opcode, so the clock is limited by the slowest instruction.
A multi-cycle design breaks each instruction into steps, allowing a shorter period at the cost of more cycles.
Modern designs are hardwired, because the opcode space is decoded once and speed matters more than flexibility.
A microcoded machine can emulate another instruction set, which is how some CPUs ran older software.

sections.title: 🧮 Clock period from the critical path
paras: Take a simple datapath: register read 80 picoseconds, ALU 250, memory access 300, register write 60. In a single-cycle design every instruction pays the sum, 690 picoseconds, so the clock tops out near 1.45 GHz even for an instruction that only adds two registers.

Break it into five cycles and drop register-to-register add to three stages: 80 + 250 + 60 = 390 picoseconds plus register overhead, so the period could be about 450 picoseconds, giving 2.2 GHz. The add still takes three cycles, but the clock is 1.5 times faster and the load instruction no longer forces every other instruction to wait for its memory access.

Now count instructions. A program of 1,000 instructions at 4 cycles each on the multi-cycle machine takes 4,000 cycles, which at 2.2 GHz is 1.8 microseconds. The same program on the single-cycle machine takes 1,000 cycles, which at 1.45 GHz is 0.69 microseconds. Fewer cycles won, despite the slower clock, because 4 cycles of overhead is a lot to pay. This is the reason designers compare cycle counts and clock rates as a product rather than separately.

sections.title: 🔍 Why overlap beats faster stages
paras: Making one stage faster has a limit: you eventually hit the speed of light through the wires. Overlapping stages has no such limit, because the work of different instructions is genuinely independent. That is why pipelines, not faster adders, delivered most of the performance gains from the 1980s onward.

The catch is that overlap only helps if there is nothing to wait for. Dependencies, branches, and cache misses all break the ideal, and the entire art of pipeline design is about keeping the pipeline full anyway.

sections.title: ⚙️ Stages, hazards, and the fixes
paras: A classic five-stage pipeline is fetch, decode, execute, memory, write-back. Five instructions are in flight at once, each at a different stage. The register file must support a read and a write in the same cycle, and the pipeline registers between stages must hold everything the next stage needs.
A hazard is anything that prevents the next instruction from issuing on schedule.
bullets: Structural hazard: two instructions want the same hardware in the same cycle, such as one fetch and one data access on a single-ported memory.
Data hazard: an instruction needs a value that a younger instruction has not written yet.
Control hazard: a branch changes which instruction should be fetched next, and the pipeline has already fetched the wrong one.
Forwarding (bypassing) fixes most data hazards by routing a result from a later stage straight to where it is needed, at the cost of extra comparators and wires.
A load-use hazard cannot be fully forwarded, because the data arrives at the end of the memory stage, so one bubble is inserted.
Branch prediction guesses the direction and speculatively executes, flushing if wrong; a mispredict costs the pipeline depth in cycles.

sections.title: 🧮 Speedup, stalls, and the branch penalty
paras: With no hazards, a five-stage pipeline retires one instruction per cycle, so the ideal speedup over a single-cycle machine is five. That is throughput, not latency: each instruction still takes five cycles from fetch to finish.

Twenty instructions: the first finishes after 5 cycles, the remaining 19 finish one per cycle, so 24 cycles instead of 100. The speedup is 4.17, not 5, because filling the pipeline costs 4 cycles of ramp-up. For 1,000 instructions the number is 1,004 cycles and the speedup is 4.98, which is why long-running code sees the ideal and short bursts do not.
Now add stalls. If one instruction in ten is a load immediately used by the next, that is one bubble per ten instructions, so 1,000 instructions take 1,100 cycles and the speedup drops to 4.5.

Add branches: with 20 percent branches and a 2-cycle mispredict penalty, a predictor that is wrong half the time costs 0.2 x 0.5 x 2 = 0.2 cycles per instruction, pushing 1,000 instructions to 1,300 cycles and the speedup to 3.8. Improving the predictor to 90 percent accuracy cuts the penalty to 0.04 cycles per instruction, which is why branch prediction research was worth billions: it recovers more performance than adding pipeline stages ever did.
